reading_head: The Distance Between a Fact and a Verdict
reading_sub: Why an investigation is written the way it is written

paras: The finding of an investigation is not a verdict, and the language it is written in exists to keep the two apart. A report may state that the sequence of events is established; it will rarely state that a person was negligent. Negligence is a legal conclusion, and it belongs to a court.

Consider three sentences about the same fact. The valve was closed. It would appear that the valve was closed before the transfer began. The witness stated that he had closed the valve. Only the first is a finding. The second is a hedge, and the reader is being told that the evidence supports it without compelling it. The third is testimony, which is what a person said. A report that mixes the three is useless to everybody who reads it afterwards.

Hedged language carries weight in the other direction as well. More often than not, a root cause is recorded as a contributing factor first, and is promoted only once the corrective action has been agreed. Investigators would rather understate a cause they cannot fully evidence than overstate one they can. The convention is deliberate: an overstated finding is attacked in court, and when it falls it takes the rest of the report down with it.

The advice given to young investigators has not changed in thirty years. If two explanations fit the evidence equally, you had better write both. If one of them can be tested, you may as well test it before you write anything at all. And if the recommendation you are about to make would have prevented this occurrence but not the next one, it seems that you have not yet found the root cause.

a hedge is not a softer way of saying the same thing: it changes what the text CLAIMS. The text states and the text implies are two different questions, and the hedge is the only mark on the page that tells them apart.

prod_sub: Two recordings, then the method in your own words

listenings.sub: A senior investigator on why she never writes the strong version. Sound first -- no text.
listenings.text: I have had two findings overturned in thirty years and I remember both of them better than anything I got right. In each case the fact was correct and the sentence was too strong. Once you write a person was negligent, you are no longer describing an event, you are making a legal claim, and somebody will come and test it. So I write it would appear that, and people outside the profession tell me that is weak. It is not weak. It is accurate about how much I know. If the evidence gets stronger later, I can promote the sentence. If I have already written the strong version, I have nowhere to go except backwards, in public. And there is a second reason nobody mentions. A hedged finding is easier for the company to accept, and a finding nobody accepts changes nothing at all.
questions: What does she remember better than anything she got right, and why?
The two findings that were overturned in thirty years. In each case the fact was correct and the sentence was too strong.
What happens, in her account, the moment you write that a person was negligent?
You stop describing an event and start making a legal claim, and somebody will come and test it.
What is the second reason she gives for hedging?
A hedged finding is easier for the company to accept, and a finding nobody accepts changes nothing at all.

listenings.sub: A safety consultant on the test that tells you the root cause is wrong. Sound first -- no text.
listenings.text: There is one question I ask about every recommendation I read, and it takes about four seconds. Would this have prevented the occurrence in front of us? Almost always yes, because people write recommendations backwards from the accident. Then I ask the second question. Would it have prevented the next one, which will not look like this one at all? And that is where most reports fall apart. If the answer is no, you have found a contributing factor and you have called it a root cause, and the corrective action you are about to agree will make everybody feel better and change nothing. I would rather send a report back three times than approve a recommendation that only works on an accident that has already happened.
questions: What is the first question he asks, and why is the answer almost always yes?
Whether the recommendation would have prevented the occurrence in front of him. Almost always yes, because people write recommendations backwards from the accident.
What is the second question, and what does a negative answer mean?
Whether it would have prevented the next one, which will not look like this one. If not, a contributing factor has been called a root cause.
What does he say he would rather do?
Send a report back three times rather than approve a recommendation that only works on an accident that has already happened.

pc_desc: The vocabulary of a formal inquiry and the hedging that separates what a text states from what it suggests. Key words: negligence, testimony, investigation, finding, recommendation, contributing factor, root cause, corrective action, witness, sequence of events. Structure: hedging language and the modals would rather, had better and may as well.

paras: It would appear that the valve was closed before the transfer began. The witness stated that he had closed it, which is testimony and not a finding. More often than not, a root cause is recorded as a contributing factor first, and to some extent that is a matter of convention rather than of evidence.

Investigators would rather understate a cause they cannot fully evidence than overstate one they can. If two explanations fit the evidence equally, you had better write both. If one of them can be tested, you may as well test it before you write anything. And if your recommendation would not prevent the next occurrence, it seems that you have not yet found the root cause.

teacher.s1: Abertura (2 min): DECISAO DE DESENHO do programa: toda aula e reading-driven, sem alternar com aula de fala (a REGRA 29.2 nao se aplica aqui), porque a prova e 100% leitura. Entre direto, sem cumprimento scriptado (REGRA 27A).
teacher.s2: Homework check + warm-up (5 min): Ela escreveu uma ordem operacional de dez linhas. Peca tres linhas e, para cada uma, QUAL prazo. Linha sem prazo e futuro perfeito sem apoio -- aponte sem corrigir o resto.
teacher.s3: Provocacao (5 min): As tres frases sao a aula inteira. Espere ela separar. Se travar, pergunte: which of the three could a witness be wrong about? (A terceira -- e testemunho, nao fato.) Este slide e o que da a ela a pergunta 'states or implies' da prova.
teacher.s4: Objetivo (2 min): Diga: the words of an inquiry, the mark that separates states from suggests, and three modals that give advice.
teacher.s5: Transicao vocab (1 min): Diga: Ten words, and four of them are ranks in the same hierarchy. Passe ao proximo.
teacher.s6: Vocab reveal 1-4 (5 min): negligence, testimony, investigation, finding. NAO traduza (REGRA 13). CCQ para testimony: If the witness is wrong, is it still testimony? (Sim -- testemunho e o que a pessoa disse, verdade ou nao.) CCQ para negligence: Can an investigation declare negligence? (Nao -- e conclusao juridica, e do tribunal.)
teacher.s7: Vocab reveal 5-7 (5 min): recommendation, contributing factor, root cause. CCQ decisivo: What is the difference between a contributing factor and a root cause? (Sem a root cause o evento NAO teria ocorrido; o contributing factor so ajudou.) Esta distincao e o coracao do listening 2.
teacher.s8: Vocab reveal 8-10 (5 min): corrective action, witness, sequence of events. CCQ para corrective action: Is it the same as precaution (Lesson 7)? (Nao -- precaution vem ANTES do evento, corrective action vem DEPOIS.) Contraste explicito: e o par que a prova gosta de trocar.
teacher.s9: Consolidate (4 min): Ela toca a palavra e le a definicao em voz alta antes de fechar o par.
teacher.s10: Transicao leitura (1 min): Diga: This text is not about an accident. It is about how accidents are written about. O proximo slide e o de TAREFA: a pergunta ANTES do texto.
teacher.s11: Leitura (7 min): Tres minutos em silencio, sem dicionario. NAO traduza. Este e o texto mais abstrato do bloco -- se ela reclamar de nao ter navio, lembre que a prova de 2025 abriu com um texto de IA. Depois UMA frase de resumo.
teacher.s12: Gist (3 min): Ela escolhe e JUSTIFICA. A opcao (a) e o assunto aparente e nao e o que o texto FAZ.
teacher.s13: True or False (7 min): REGRA DA CASA: TRUE ou FALSE e DEPOIS a linha que prova. A afirmacao 2 e a que decide a aula: 'it would appear that' NAO e finding.
teacher.s14: Transicao gramatica (1 min): Diga: Now the three words that did all that work. Passe ao proximo.
teacher.s15: Grammar discovery (7 min): Nao de a regra. Peca que ela TIRE o hedge do exemplo 1 e leia de novo -- e depois diga do que o autor deixou de ser responsavel. So entao clique Reveal the Rule. CCQ decisivo: does 'it would appear that X' mean X is true? (Nao -- significa que a evidencia aponta para X.) Ela estuda gramatica sozinha: aqui e ferramenta de leitura.
teacher.s16: Practice (4 min): Ela diz a forma ORALMENTE antes de clicar.
teacher.s17: Spot the error (4 min): A primeira frase erra de SENTIDO (o hedge nao autoriza a certeza) e as tres seguintes erram de FORMA (to depois de would rather / had better, -ing depois de may as well). Diga isso antes.
teacher.s18: Transicao equivalencia (1 min): Diga: Same method, other words. Passe ao proximo.
teacher.s19: Como a prova esconde (4 min): O primeiro par e o mais perigoso do programa: 'it would appear that the valve was closed' -> 'the evidence points to the valve having been closed'. Os dois sao hedges, e uma terceira versao ('the valve was closed') nao seria equivalente. Faca ela dizer por que.
teacher.s20: Equivalencia (5 min): Depois de fechar os pares, cubra a direita e faca a direcao dificil.
teacher.s21: Complete (5 min): Teacher-led, uma lacuna por vez. As oito respostas sao oito das dez palavras da aula.
teacher.s22: Quick fire (6 min): Uma por vez, em voz alta, antes das dicas. A ultima ensina o procedimento: para responder 'states or implies', PROCURE O HEDGE na pagina.
teacher.s23: Transicao (1 min): Diga: Somebody who writes them, and somebody who sends them back. Passe ao proximo.
teacher.s24: Listening 1 (5 min): LEIA AS 3 PERGUNTAS EM VOZ ALTA COM ELA ANTES de tocar (REGRA 2.1). Escuta medida em 0%: 0.75x na primeira vez. A frase 'It is accurate about how much I know' e a definicao de hedge em uma linha -- volte a ela.
teacher.s25: Listening 2 (5 min): LEIA AS 3 PERGUNTAS EM VOZ ALTA COM ELA ANTES de tocar (REGRA 2.1). Este audio e o teste operacional de root cause. Peca que ela repita as DUAS perguntas dele sem olhar.
teacher.s26: Role-play guiado (4 min): Cinco frases com os frames. Conte quantos hedges corretos ela produz.
teacher.s27: Role-play semi-livre (5 min): Regra dura: ela nao pode responder de memoria, tem de APONTAR as palavras. E o treino direto da questao states/implies.
teacher.s28: Producao livre (6 min): Nao interrompa. Mede-se: quatro frases corretamente separadas e a evidencia nomeada para os dois hedges.
teacher.s29: Transicao wrap-up (1 min): Diga: Let us see what you can do now.
teacher.s30: Survival card (3 min): Cinco frases do proprio texto. Insista em 'would rather' -- na fala vira /wʊdrɑːðə/ quase colado, e e assim que ela vai ouvir.
teacher.s31: Checklist (2 min): Leia cada item em voz alta. Os 5 checks fecham a aula e acendem o stamp.
teacher.s32: Encerramento (2 min): Diga: Lesson 9 complete, Helena.
